Hinge Romance Scam UK: How to Spot Fake Profiles and Protect Yourself

Hinge romance scammers spend weeks building trust before asking for money — here's how to spot them before you lose anything.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-14 · 9 min read

Hinge romance scam UKfake Hinge profilesdating app scamromance scammer warning signsHinge catfish scam
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Report Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What is a Hinge romance scam?

A Hinge romance scam is when someone creates a fake profile on the dating app Hinge to build a romantic relationship with you, with the sole aim of extracting money. The scammer typically spends weeks or months chatting with you, building emotional trust and sometimes moving conversations off the app to messaging platforms like WhatsApp or Telegram. Once they have established what feels like a genuine connection, they introduce a financial emergency — a medical bill, a business problem, travel costs, or a supposed investment opportunity — and ask you to send money.

Some scammers ask for smaller amounts repeatedly; others request a large lump sum. The money is transferred to the scammer's bank account or cryptocurrency wallet, and once sent, it is almost never recovered. The scammer then either disappears or continues the relationship while asking for more money.

Red flags that reveal a Hinge romance scammer

  • **Reluctance to video call or meet in person.** They make excuses (poor internet, work travel, family emergency) whenever you suggest a video call or in-person meeting, even after weeks of chatting.
  • **Suspiciously perfect photos.** Their pictures look professionally shot, are unusually attractive, or reverse-image search results show the photos belong to someone else or appear on modelling websites.
  • **Rapid emotional escalation.** They say 'I love you' or talk about a future together within days or weeks, moving much faster than a genuine relationship would.
  • **Vague or inconsistent personal details.** Their job, location, family background, or life story changes slightly each time they mention it, or they avoid answering direct questions about themselves.
  • **Requests to move off Hinge quickly.** They push to continue conversations on WhatsApp, Telegram, or email within the first few days, claiming Hinge is unreliable or they prefer privacy.
  • **Financial requests disguised as emergencies.** They suddenly mention a crisis — a sick relative, a business deal gone wrong, unexpected travel costs — and ask you to send money urgently.
  • **Requests for money via untraceable methods.** They ask you to pay via bank transfer, cryptocurrency, gift cards, or money transfer apps rather than through Hinge's own payment system (if available).
  • **Isolation tactics.** They discourage you from telling friends or family about the relationship, or they ask you to keep the financial help secret.

How the scam unfolds from first message to money loss

The scam typically begins with a well-crafted profile that appeals to your preferences — attractive photos, a job that sounds impressive, interests that match yours. The scammer sends you a message that feels personal and genuine, often referencing something from your profile. Over the next few weeks, they engage in regular, warm conversation. They ask about your day, share stories about their life, and gradually build emotional intimacy. They may send you voice messages or claim to be planning a visit to meet you. During this time, they are learning about your financial situation, your values, and your vulnerabilities.

Once they judge the moment is right, they introduce a crisis. A parent has fallen ill and they need money for medical treatment. A business deal has collapsed and they need funds to recover. They are stuck abroad and need help with a flight home. They ask you to send money as a sign of your commitment to the relationship, or they frame it as a temporary loan they will repay. You send the money via bank transfer, cryptocurrency, or a money transfer app. The scammer receives it, and the account or wallet is emptied or closed.

They may disappear entirely, or they may continue the relationship and ask for more money, claiming the first payment didn't solve the problem.

How to verify if a Hinge match is genuine

**Use reverse image search on their photos.** Right-click on their profile pictures and search them on Google Images, TinEye, or Yandex. If the same photos appear on modelling websites, stock photo sites, or other dating profiles under different names, the profile is fake. **Ask for a video call early.** Genuine matches will usually agree to a video call within the first week or two. If they consistently refuse or make excuses, that is a strong warning sign. **Check their social media.** Ask for their Instagram, Facebook, or LinkedIn.

A real person will have an established presence with a history of posts and connections. A scammer's accounts are often brand new, have very few followers, or do not exist. **Ask specific questions about their life.** Request details about their job, hometown, family, or hobbies. Genuine people give consistent, detailed answers; scammers often give vague replies or their story changes. **Verify their location.** If they claim to be in the UK, ask them about local landmarks, current events, or specific details about their area.

Scammers often cannot answer these convincingly. **Be wary of requests to move off Hinge.** Hinge's platform includes safety features and reporting tools. Scammers want to move conversations to unmonitored platforms like WhatsApp or Telegram where they cannot be reported as easily. **Never send money before meeting in person.** This is the single most important rule. A genuine match will understand why you will not send money to someone you have not met face-to-face.

What to do immediately if you have already sent money

If you have already transferred money to a scammer, act quickly. **Contact your bank or payment provider right away.** Call the number on the back of your card or use the official app. Tell them you have been scammed and ask if the transaction can be stopped or reversed. If the money was sent via bank transfer, your bank may be able to recall it if the recipient has not yet withdrawn it. **Report the transaction as fraud.** Your bank will guide you through this process.

Keep all evidence — screenshots of messages, profile details, and transaction records. **If you used a money transfer app or cryptocurrency,** contact the service's support team immediately. Some services can freeze accounts or reverse transactions if reported quickly enough. **Block the scammer on Hinge and any other platforms** where you have been in contact. Do not respond to any further messages. **Report the profile to Hinge.** Use the app's reporting feature to flag the account as a scam.

This helps protect other users. **Do not send any more money,** even if the scammer claims they will repay you or that the first payment was not enough. This is a common tactic to extract additional funds.

Reporting a Hinge romance scam in the UK

**Report to Hinge directly.** Open the profile, tap the three-dot menu, and select 'Report'. Describe the scam clearly and provide screenshots. Hinge takes these reports seriously and will investigate. **Report to Action Fraud (Report Fraud).** Call 0300 123 2040 or visit reportfraud.org.uk. This is the UK's national fraud reporting service. They will create a record of the scam and may investigate if it is part of a larger pattern. **Report to the NCSC if you received phishing emails or links.** Forward suspicious emails to report@phishing.gov.uk.

If the scammer sent you a link claiming to verify your identity or access a fake Hinge login page, this is particularly important. **Forward any suspicious text messages to 7726.** If the scammer contacted you via SMS, forward the message to this free reporting number. **Contact Citizens Advice.** Call their consumer helpline on 0808 223 1133 for guidance on next steps and support. **Keep detailed records.** Save all screenshots, messages, profile information, and transaction details.

These will be needed if you pursue a chargeback with your bank or if the case is investigated. **Consider reporting to the police.** If a large sum of money was involved, you can report the scam to your local police force via their non-emergency number or online reporting tool, though they may have limited resources for individual cases.

Frequently asked questions

How can I tell if a Hinge profile is fake before I get emotionally invested?

Check their photos using reverse image search, ask for a video call within the first week, and verify their social media accounts. Real people will have established Instagram or Facebook profiles with a history of posts. Scammers often refuse video calls, have brand-new social media accounts, or their photos appear on modelling websites under different names. If something feels off, trust your instinct and move on.

I've already sent money to someone I met on Hinge. Can I get it back?

Contact your bank or payment provider immediately — they may be able to stop or reverse the transaction if it has not been withdrawn yet. Report the fraud to your bank, Action Fraud (0300 123 2040), and Hinge itself. If you used a money transfer app or cryptocurrency, contact that service's support team urgently. The sooner you act, the better your chances of recovery, though in many cases the money cannot be retrieved once it has been sent.

What should I do if a Hinge match asks me to move our conversation to WhatsApp or Telegram?

Be cautious. Scammers often push to move conversations off Hinge because the app has safety features and reporting tools. A genuine match will not mind staying on Hinge for a while, and they will understand if you want to meet in person before moving to private messaging. If they insist on moving off the app very quickly, or if they become evasive when you ask why, that is a red flag.

Is it safe to give a Hinge match my phone number or social media details?

Giving your phone number or social media handle is generally lower risk than sending money, but be cautious. Scammers may use your details to impersonate you on other platforms or to build a more convincing fake identity. Only share these details after you have verified the person is genuine — ideally after a video call or in-person meeting. Never share your full address, workplace details, or financial information until you are certain the person is who they claim to be.

What if the person I'm chatting with seems genuine but asks for money for a business investment or cryptocurrency opportunity?

This is almost always a scam, even if the person seems trustworthy and the opportunity sounds legitimate. Genuine romantic partners do not ask for money for investments, especially not early in a relationship. Scammers often use investment schemes because they sound more credible than emergency requests. Never send money for any investment, business opportunity, or financial scheme to someone you have not met in person and known for a long time. If they pressure you or become defensive when you ask questions, that is a clear warning sign.
